## About this session

This session is a free-standing introduction to [duckdb in R](https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/clients/r). In this session, we'll use the `duckdb` package as a database back-end, and demonstrate how to interact with that back-end using the DBI package. You might also be interested in [our session on dbplyr](r_training/dbplyr_dtplyr.html) as an alternative means of using your duckdb database.


::: {.callout-tip collapse="false" appearance="default" icon="true"}
## Session resources
+ you'll need a reasonable working knowledge of R to enjoy this session
+ no special infrastructure requirements other than a recent-ish R setup
+ see the setup chunk below for package requirements

:::

## Setup

Create a new project, and install and attach packages:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# install.packages("pak")
# pak::pak("duckdb")
# pak::pak("DBI")
# pak::pak("palmerpenguins")

library(duckdb)
library(dplyr) # surprisingly useful for working with databases
library(DBI)
library(palmerpenguins)

mini_pengs <- penguins |>
  select(species, island, sex, year, bill_length_mm) |>
  slice_sample(n = 5) # create a mini dataset of penguins
```
:::


## What?

Duckdb is a lightweight database backend that allows you to create comparatively high-performance databases on your local computer easily. That comes with two main advantages:

1. It's a neat way of porting SQL projects to R, or allowing SQL-fluent colleagues to avoid having to relearn everything in R
1. It's a great way of managing inconveniently large data on the desktop, or in other situations where resources are scarce

Here's the minimal example:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mem_con <- dbConnect(duckdb()) 
```
:::


This connection object represents an in-memory duckdb database. To add some data to that database, we can use `duckdb::dbWriteTable`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
duckdb::dbWriteTable(conn = mem_con, name = "pengs", value = mini_pengs)

# dplyr::copy_to(dest = mem_con,df = penguins, name = "mini_pengs") # just beware the names (and order) of arguments differs from the otherwise-similar dplyr::copy_to function
```
:::


There are then a range of options for retrieving data. `DBI::dbGetQuery` executes a SQL query on your database, and returns a standard R data.frame:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
DBI::dbGetQuery(mem_con, "SELECT * FROM pengs")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
    species island    sex year bill_length_mm
1    Gentoo Biscoe   male 2008           49.5
2    Gentoo Biscoe   male 2009           50.8
3 Chinstrap  Dream female 2008           46.2
4    Gentoo Biscoe   male 2008           46.2
5    Gentoo Biscoe female 2009           46.9
```


:::
:::


That allows you to execute any ordinary SQL query, although we'll keep those very simple in this session:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
DBI::dbGetQuery(mem_con, "SELECT * FROM pengs WHERE species = 'Adelie'")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] species        island         sex            year           bill_length_mm
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
```


:::
:::


You can also do much the same thing without writing SQL with the combination of dplyr and [dbplyr](r_training/dbplyr_dtplyr.html):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tbl(mem_con, "pengs") |>
  filter(species == "Adelie") |>
  collect() # collecting data from the query and returning a tibble
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 0 × 5
# ℹ 5 variables: species <fct>, island <fct>, sex <fct>, year <int>,
#   bill_length_mm <dbl>
```


:::
:::


## On-disk databases

Our duckDB database so far has lived in memory. Ideal for demo purposes, not great for durable production use. Luckily, we can write duckDB databases to disk. The substantive change is to supply a filepath for your database to `dbConnect`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
disk_con <- dbConnect(duckdb(), dbdir = "data/disk_con.duckdb") 
```
:::


Then write a table to that on-disk database:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
duckdb::dbWriteTable(conn = disk_con, name = "pengs", value = mini_pengs)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

:::


Which can then be queried in the usual way:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
DBI::dbGetQuery(disk_con, "SELECT * FROM pengs WHERE species = 'Adelie'")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] species        island         sex            year           bill_length_mm
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
DBI::dbListTables(disk_con)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "pengs"
```


:::
:::



## Referencing tibbles/data.frames

Like creating a virtual table. Doesn't copy any data, good for practice and preview.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
duckdb_register(mem_con, "ref_pengs", mini_pengs)

DBI::dbGetQuery(mem_con, "SELECT * FROM ref_pengs WHERE species = 'Adelie'")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] species        island         sex            year           bill_length_mm
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
```


:::
:::


## Big chunky data

Scotland makes available national prescribing data [aggregated by dispenser and by medication type](https://www.opendata.nhs.scot/dataset/prescriptions-in-the-community/resource/15e675c7-ac8d-4000-a690-b70a2d3d3a76). That full data-set is pretty chunky indeed - roughly a couple of million rows of data per month, which is probably a bit larger than we can comfortably deal with in a training session, so we'll use a slice of this data showing prescriptions in NHS Grampian to explore DuckDB as a tool for working with big(ish) data.

Here's some data-wranging code, which probably isn't going to be of interest:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
# dispensers_2026july <- phsopendata::get_resource("15e675c7-ac8d-4000-a690-b70a2d3d3a76") |>
#   filter(HBT == "S08000020") # grab your Grampian

# dispensers_2026july |>
# readr::write_rds(here::here("r_training/data/dispensers_2026july.rds"))
```
:::


You should [download the sample data](data/dispensers_2026july.rds) - approximately 200MB - and save it somewhere sensible in your current R project. We can then read that data as a tibble, which we can then register into our on-disk DB


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
data_path <- "r_training/data/dispensers_2026july.rds" # change that to suit

dispensers_2026july <- readr::read_rds(here::here(data_path))

# disk_con <- dbConnect(duckdb(), dbdir = "data/disk_con.duckdb") # if you didn't set-up an on-disk DB above

duckdb_register(disk_con, "dispensers_2026july", dispensers_2026july, overwrite = T) # otherwise overwriting a table causes duckdb_register to fail
```
:::



## Simple filter and summarise

We could do that in dplyr:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dispensers_2026july |>
  filter(stringr::str_detect(BNFItemCode, "0209000A0AAA")) |>
  summarise(.by = c(BNFItemCode, BNFItemDescription), PaidQuantity = sum(PaidQuantity))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  BNFItemCode     BNFItemDescription                    PaidQuantity
  <chr>           <chr>                                        <dbl>
1 0209000A0AAAKAK ASPIRIN 75MG GASTRO-RESISTANT TABLETS       45647 
2 0209000A0AAAJAJ ASPIRIN 75MG TABLETS                        30162 
3 0209000A0AAABAB ASPIRIN 75MG DISPERSIBLE TABLETS           573612.
```


:::
:::


Here's the SQL version:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
DBI::dbGetQuery(disk_con, "SELECT BNFItemCode, BNFItemDescription, SUM(PaidQuantity) AS PaidQuantity,  FROM dispensers_2026july WHERE BNFItemCode LIKE '0209000A0AAA%' GROUP BY BNFItemCode, BNFItemDescription")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      BNFItemCode                    BNFItemDescription PaidQuantity
1 0209000A0AAABAB      ASPIRIN 75MG DISPERSIBLE TABLETS     573612.3
2 0209000A0AAAJAJ                  ASPIRIN 75MG TABLETS      30162.0
3 0209000A0AAAKAK ASPIRIN 75MG GASTRO-RESISTANT TABLETS      45647.0
```


:::
:::


Or a transitional form using dbplyr:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tbl(disk_con, "dispensers_2026july") |>
  filter(stringr::str_detect(BNFItemCode, "0209000A0AAA")) |>
  summarise(.by = c(BNFItemCode, BNFItemDescription), PaidQuantity = sum(PaidQuantity)) |>
  collect()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  BNFItemCode     BNFItemDescription                    PaidQuantity
  <chr>           <chr>                                        <dbl>
1 0209000A0AAABAB ASPIRIN 75MG DISPERSIBLE TABLETS           573612.
2 0209000A0AAAJAJ ASPIRIN 75MG TABLETS                        30162 
3 0209000A0AAAKAK ASPIRIN 75MG GASTRO-RESISTANT TABLETS       45647 
```


:::
:::


## Benchmarking


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
library(microbenchmark)

presc_bench <- microbenchmark::microbenchmark(

  dplyr = dispensers_2026july |>
    filter(stringr::str_detect(BNFItemCode, "0209000A0AAA")) |>
    summarise(.by = c(BNFItemCode, BNFItemDescription), PaidQuantity = sum(PaidQuantity)),
  
  sql = DBI::dbGetQuery(disk_con, "SELECT BNFItemCode, BNFItemDescription, SUM(PaidQuantity) AS PaidQuantity,  FROM dispensers_2026july WHERE BNFItemCode LIKE '0209000A0AAA%' GROUP BY BNFItemCode, BNFItemDescription"),

  dbplyr = tbl(disk_con, "dispensers_2026july") |>
    filter(stringr::str_detect(BNFItemCode, "0209000A0AAA")) |>
    summarise(.by = c(BNFItemCode, BNFItemDescription), PaidQuantity = sum(PaidQuantity)) |>
    collect()
)

presc_bench |>
  readr::write_rds(here::here("r_training/data/presc_bench.rds")) |>
  autoplot()
```
:::
